## Learning objectives

- separate aggregates, events, and projections
- build a denormalized view from duplicate or reordered events
- expose absence, partial state, and freshness to Angular
- distinguish conceptual rebuildability from an available replay source
- explain a future transition from Lists to Streams or an event store

## Aggregate versus projection

| Insurance aggregate | Rental query projection |
|---|---|
| Owns acceptance invariant | Owns no business command |
| Source of truth for insurance | Derived from service events |
| Must not be deleted casually | Disposable if inputs can be replayed |
| Optimized for business change | Optimized for `GET by rentalId` |

The databases are separate: `insurance.insurance_offers` and
`rental_query.rental_views`. Collection ownership is never shared.

## Event-fed architecture

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  Rental[carRental] -->|AuctionWon v1| Router[Redis List router]
  Insurance[insuranceService] -->|Proposed / Accepted v1| Router
  Router --> Ready[[rental-query ready]]
  Ready --> Projector[rentalQueryService]
  Projector --> Archive[(projection_event_archive)]
  Projector --> View[(rental_query.rental_views)]
  Angular -->|GET by rentalId| Projector
  Angular -->|accept command| Insurance
```

## Query-shaped denormalization

One document groups rental, vehicle, price, discount, insurance, event
identities, and timestamps. Duplication removes front-end joins and
cross-service availability coupling from the read path.

The cost is propagation lag, storage, projector code, monitoring, and a repair
obligation. A convenient projection never becomes the source of truth.

## Idempotence and duplicates

At-least-once handling means a database commit can be followed by a crash
before List acknowledgement. The same envelope will return.

- the append-only archive has a unique `event_id` index;
- archive insert and view update share one MongoDB transaction;
- a repeated `eventId` produces no second update;
- `rental_id` is unique;
- acknowledgement follows the MongoDB commit.

## Events can arrive out of order

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
  participant Q as Query projector
  participant M as MongoDB view
  Q->>M: InsuranceOfferAccepted (create partial view)
  Q->>M: AuctionWon (fill rental fields)
  Q->>M: InsuranceOfferProposed (fill proposal metadata)
  Note over M: status remains ACCEPTED
```

Insurance events carry enough data for a partial component. Accepted never
regresses to proposed. Per-component timestamps prevent stale replacement.

## Eventual consistency is API behavior

`GET /rental-views/{rentalId}` may return:

- `404` before the first event is projected;
- `PARTIAL` when insurance arrived before rental facts;
- `COMPLETE` with no insurance yet because insurance is optional;
- later, the same view with `PROPOSED` or `ACCEPTED` insurance.

Angular polls for a bounded time and keeps insurance knowledge in its extension.

## Rebuildability: three different claims

1. **Conceptual:** projector code is deterministic and order tolerant.
2. **Transport reality:** consumed Redis Lists retain no replayable history.
3. **Durable source:** `projection_event_archive` retains raw accepted inputs.
4. **Operational rebuild:** disable consumption, delete only `rental_views`,
   and replay the archive. NDJSON imports cover pre-archive history.

The archive has no TTL. Pruning requires a verified snapshot and replay boundary.

## Failure classification

- malformed or unsupported events move atomically to a service-specific DLQ;
- MongoDB or Redis failures remain recoverable in `processing`;
- DLQ entries retain the original payload and diagnostic context;
- operators alert, repair, and explicitly replay or discard each entry.

## What a retained log adds later

Redis Streams, evaluated in a separate project, add transport IDs, consumer
groups, pending inspection, and replay within configured retention. An event
store adds domain-grade, long-term immutable history.

Neither automatically solves schema evolution, poison events, ordering rules,
or side-effect idempotence.

## CQRS without event sourcing

The implementation separates command owners from a read model: a CQRS shape.
It is not Event Sourcing because aggregates remain current state and Redis Lists
are not an authoritative history.
